title: Comment Window Closes on Plan to End Deference for H-1B Extensions
excerpt: DHS proposes deleting the one regulation that tells USCIS to respect a prior approval when an extension changes nothing. The rule is still in force, and a final decision comes next.
body:
• The public comment period on the proposal to end deference for work-visa extensions closed on November 13, 2026. Nothing has changed yet: the deference regulation stays in force unless DHS publishes a final rule.
  • The proposal would delete 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), the sentence that tells USCIS to respect a prior approval on a Form I-129 extension involving the same employer, the same worker and the same facts.
  • DHS estimates about 208,429 extension petitions a year would lose deference, and about 6,044 more requests for evidence a year would follow. H-1B petitions make up more than 75% of Form I-129 filings.
  • If your extension is pending or coming up, it is still decided under today's rule. There is nothing to file now; the next step is DHS publishing a final rule, and no date for one has been set.

The Department of Homeland Security wants to strike one sentence from the immigration regulations, and the public record on that proposal is now closed. The notice of proposed rulemaking, titled “Removing Deference to Prior USCIS Determinations of Eligibility,” was published in the Federal Register on October 14, 2026 (91 FR 65119, docket USCIS-2026-0529). Comments were due on or before November 13, 2026, through the Federal eRulemaking Portal at regulations.gov. DHS must now consider the comments before deciding whether to issue a final rule.

Who is affected, exactly

The proposal reaches every extension filed on Form I-129, the petition employers use for nonimmigrant workers: H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN, E and P classifications among them. It bites only where an employer asks to extend a worker on the same terms USCIS already approved — the same parties and the same underlying facts. First-time petitions are not affected; they never carried deference and already get a full review. Workers whose status is not being extended are not affected either.

Counted here: the roughly 208,429 extension petitions a year that DHS estimates would lose the benefit of deference. Not counted: new petitions, and extensions where the job or employer has materially changed, which officers can already re-examine under the current rule's exceptions.

What would change

Today, 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) tells a USCIS officer reviewing an extension with the same parties and the same facts to defer to the earlier approval. The officer may depart from it only for a material error in the prior approval, a material change in circumstances or eligibility requirements, or new material information that hurts eligibility. When an officer does not defer, current guidance requires the officer to acknowledge the prior approval, explain why, obtain supervisory approval and give the petitioner a chance to respond.

The proposal deletes that paragraph and leaves it marked “[Reserved].” An extension for the same employer, the same worker and the same job would then be reviewed as if USCIS had never approved it before. The officer could still look at the prior approval as evidence, but would not be required to start from it, and the procedural safeguards around departing from it would disappear with the regulation, according to an analysis by Reddy Neumann Brown PC. Deference never guaranteed approval — petitioners still file a complete extension with evidence — but it stopped officers from re-deciding settled questions, such as whether the same job is a specialty occupation, when nothing had changed.

Why DHS wants the change, and what its own data shows

DHS gives three reasons in the proposal: the burden of proof under the Immigration and Nationality Act sits with the petitioner, and deference shifts it to the officer; deference can discourage officers from issuing requests for evidence (RFEs) when eligibility has not been proven; and a questionable first approval can become an anchor for later filings.

The proposal's own numbers are narrower than its reach. DHS states that denial rates did not statistically differ between periods with and without deference, and its analysis found no change in denials at all. The measurable effect it found was more RFEs: about 6,044 additional ones a year. Each RFE adds work and time; lawyers analysing the department's figures estimate one added RFE can add about 64 days to a case. Longer processing matters beyond the wait itself — a timely filed H-1B extension lets the worker keep working for up to 240 days after the I-94 expires, and workers often delay travel abroad for a new visa stamp until an extension is approved.

Who feels it most

H-1B petitions make up more than 75% of all Form I-129 filings, according to DHS, so H-1B workers would feel the change most. Indian professionals would be at the centre of it: USCIS's FY 2025 report to Congress put workers born in India at 77.6% of H-1B approvals for continuing employment. The burden would not fall only on large technology employers. DHS found that 57% of the employers it could classify that filed H-1B extensions in FY 2025 were small entities, and the median small entity filed just one petition.

A rule that has come and gone before

Deference began as a 2004 USCIS memorandum, was rescinded in October 2017, and was reinstated in the USCIS Policy Manual in April 2021. DHS then wrote it into the regulations in the H-1B Modernization Final Rule of December 2024, effective January 17, 2025. Lawyers who lived through the 2017–2021 period recall routine extensions for the same job drawing RFEs that re-litigated questions USCIS had already approved. Less than two years after codifying deference, DHS now proposes to undo it.

What to do next

Nothing, yet — and that is the operative fact. The comment deadline was not an effective date, the proposal sets no date for a final rule, and 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) remains in force while DHS reviews the comments. Extensions filed now are decided under the rule that exists today. What to watch is the Federal Register: a final rule, if one comes, will be published there with its own effective date, and employers planning extensions in 2027 should budget for fuller evidence files and longer timelines if it is adopted as proposed.
